traveler: Chiara di Favarone di Offreduccio (Clare of Assisi)
title: One Wall for Forty-One Years: Clare of Assisi and the Privilege of Owning Nothing
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House Beside the Bell Tower

stops.name: Assisi, the Offreduccio house behind San Rufino
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The year 1194 and the day 16 July are a later attribution, not fixed by any contemporary document; the Catholic Encyclopedia and Wikipedia both carry the date while noting it is unestablished. Fortini's documentary biography was not reachable in this pass to check it against the Assisi notarial record.
stops.campa: Behind the bell tower of San Rufino stands the fortified house of the Offreduccio, a family of knights who hold land, towers, and the right to bear arms. To Favarone and his wife Ortolana a daughter is born and named Chiara, the clear one. Ortolana has been to Rome, to Monte Gargano, and over the sea to Jerusalem, and comes back to a city where the noble families keep their doors barred and their sons in mail. The child is raised toward a dowry and a marriage her family will arrange for her when the time comes to arrange one. Nothing in the record suggests anyone in the house expects otherwise.
suggested_refs: The fortified house beside the campanile of San Rufino, identified as the Offreduccio dwelling

stops.name: Assisi, the font in the right aisle
stops.date_confidence: inferred. Baptism at San Rufino is attested by the cathedral's own tradition and the atlas already carries the claim from two other files; the day is assumed to follow the traditional birth date and is nowhere documented.
stops.campa: She is carried down into the cathedral and christened at the font in the right aisle. The same basin has already taken Francis, son of the cloth merchant Pietro di Bernardone, a dozen years before her, and tradition adds the infant Frederick of Hohenstaufen to the list. Nothing in the water distinguishes the three. Assisi is a small city and its font is one stone bowl, and every soul born inside the walls comes through it. The bowl is still standing in the right aisle, and visitors are still shown it.
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'Assisi, Cathedral of San Rufino, the baptism'
suggested_refs: The baptismal font of San Rufino, still shown to visitors as the font of Francis and Clare

stops.name: Assisi, the Rocca pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1198 uprising and the destruction of the fortress; no source names the Offreduccio among the families dispossessed, and Clare's own situation in that year is undocumented. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The emperor's garrison holds the fortress on the hill above the town. In 1198 the commune rises, storms it, and pulls the walls down stone by stone, and with them the legal footing of every family that holds its rank from the empire. The Offreduccio are maiores: knights, not merchants. Clare is four years old in the year her own class is dispossessed by its neighbours. Then the men of the popolo come for the towers of the maiores, and they burn them and level them, one street of the town at a time.
suggested_refs: The Rocca Maggiore above Assisi, razed in the communal revolt of 1198 and rebuilt in 1367

stops.name: Perugia, the years among the enemy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The refuge of Assisi's nobles in Perugia is standard in the biographies, but no fetched source places the Offreduccio there and none places Clare there at any date. Month and day are an ordering device only.
stops.campa: The dispossessed nobles of Assisi go over the hills to Perugia, the rival city, which is glad to shelter anyone who will be trouble for Assisi later. The Offreduccio are said to be among them, and Clare to have spent part of her childhood in that exile, though no document puts her inside the walls of Perugia on any day. What is certain is the war that follows. In 1202 the two cities meet at Collestrada and Assisi is broken, and the young men taken there sit a year in Perugian cellars. One of them is Francis di Bernardone.
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stops 'Collestrada, the battle with Perugia' and 'Perugia, the year in the pits'
suggested_refs: Siméon Luce and the Assisi communal record for the 1198-1203 conflict between maiores and popolo

stops.name: Assisi, the marriage proposed and refused
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The episode of the marriage offered at about twelve and deferred to eighteen comes from the hagiographic tradition as summarised on Wikipedia; the year is calculated from the traditional birth date. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The families come back under the peace the two classes swear between them, and the ordinary business of a noble house resumes. Clare is about twelve when her parents open negotiations for her marriage. She asks to be left until she is eighteen. Her mother Ortolana, who has walked to Jerusalem, does not force her. Her uncle Monaldo heads the family in her father's place, and what he thinks of the delay is not recorded. The girl gives away food out of the house and will not wear what her rank requires her to wear.
suggested_refs: The depositions of Bona di Guelfuccio and Pacifica di Guelfuccio in the 1253 process of canonisation

stops.name: Assisi, the preacher in Lent
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the venue is contradicted. Wikipedia's article on the cathedral places the sermon that starts her vocation at San Rufino; Wikipedia's article on Clare places it at San Giorgio. Neither is resolved here. The date is a placement inside Lent 1212 and is not documented.
stops.campa: The merchant's son who stripped himself naked in the bishop's square is now preaching Lent in Assisi, in the vernacular, to whoever will stand and listen. Clare hears him. She is standing in a church she has been brought to since she could walk, listening to a man her family regards as a lunatic. Which church is not settled: the account attached to the cathedral puts the sermon at San Rufino, forty paces from her father's door, and the account attached to her own life puts it at San Giorgio, down the hill. Nothing reconciles the two.
suggested_refs: The church of San Giorgio, Assisi, the alternative site of the Lenten sermon, later absorbed into the Basilica of Santa Chiara

stops.name: Assisi, the meetings arranged through Brother Philip
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The go-between Philip and the chaperone Bona di Guelfuccio come from the 1253 canonisation testimony, which was not fetched in a primary edition for this file; the dating to the weeks before the flight is inference from the flight itself.
stops.campa: She sends for him. The go-between is Brother Philip, and she is chaperoned by Bona di Guelfuccio, a woman of her own household who will be questioned about it under oath forty-one years later. They meet in secret because the alternative is a signed contract of marriage. Francis tells her what he tells everyone: sell what you have, give it away, follow. Nobody else in Assisi is saying that to a girl of her rank, and nobody else has anywhere to send her. He tells her where to go and on what night.
suggested_refs: Regis J. Armstrong, ed., Clare of Assisi: Early Documents. The Lady (New City Press, 2006), for the canonisation depositions

stops.name: Assisi, the door of the dead
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the pool's own date is wrong. Palm Sunday 1212 in the Julian calendar fell on 18 March, not 20 March, which was a Tuesday; Julian Easter 1212 was 25 March. Fortini prefers Palm Sunday 1211, that is 27 March 1211. The entire Palm Sunday departure narrative appears only in the Legend of Saint Clare and in none of Clare's own writings.
stops.campa: On the night after Palm Sunday she leaves. The Legend says she goes out through the door of the dead, the small walled-up opening in the front of a noble house that is unblocked only to carry a coffin into the street, and that she and her companions clear the stones from it with their hands. Her aunt Bianca goes with her, and one other woman. The whole of this scene stands on a text written more than forty years afterward by men who were not in the house. She never mentions the door in anything she wrote herself.
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Chiara d'Assisi' ('Il racconto della Domenica delle Palme e presente solo nella leggenda di Chiara')
Legend of Saint Clare, c. 1255-56, via secondary summary
suggested_refs: Thomas of Celano (attrib.), Legenda Sanctae Clarae Virginis, c. 1255-56

stops.name: Porziuncola, the shears in the torchlight
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Placed on the night following Palm Sunday 1212, corrected from the propagated '20 March 1212'. Some scholarship moves the whole episode to 1211. saint_francis.journey.json dates the same scene 1212-03-18; the one-day offset here is only the difference between leaving the house and arriving at the chapel.
stops.campa: A mile out on the plain, in the wood around the little chapel of Santa Maria degli Angeli, the friars are waiting with torches. Francis cuts off her hair. She puts down the dress she walked out of Assisi in and takes a rough tunic and a cord, and there is now, in law and in fact, no marriage that can be made for her. The community she has just joined is made up entirely of men, living in a hut on the plain, with no provision of any kind for a woman who has done this. She is eighteen years old.
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Saint Clare of Assisi': 'St. Francis, having cut off her hair, clothed her in a rough tunic'
saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'Porziuncola, Clare's flight and tonsure'
suggested_refs: The Porziuncola chapel, now enclosed inside the Basilica di Santa Maria degli Angeli

stops.name: Bastia Umbra, San Paolo delle Abbadesse: the hands on the altar cloth
stops.date_confidence: attested for the reception at San Paolo in 1212 (it.wikipedia, 'Bastia Umbra'); the day is inferred from the tonsure. The altar-clinging and the shorn head shown to the kinsmen are Legend material. Coordinate corrected to the church by the municipal cemetery at the Tescio-Chiascio confluence, some 1.9 km from the figure in the research pool.
stops.campa: Before dawn the friars walk her down to a Benedictine house of nuns by the confluence of the Tescio and the Chiascio, where the abbess holds the right of sanctuary. The Offreduccio men arrive within days: uncles, cousins, armed and entitled, offering argument first and then force. She takes hold of the altar cloth and will not be moved, and when they keep on she pulls back her veil and shows them the shorn head. Under canon law the argument is finished at that moment. They ride back to Assisi without her.
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Bastia Umbra' (reception of Clare, 1212; church at the Tescio-Chiascio confluence, annexed to the 1862 cemetery)
OpenStreetMap Nominatim, 'Chiesa di San Paolo delle Abbadesse, Bastia Umbra'
suggested_refs: The church of San Paolo delle Abbadesse, Bastia Umbra, now beside the municipal cemetery

stops.name: Sant'Angelo di Panzo, the second house
stops.date_confidence: attested that she moved to Sant'Angelo di Panzo in 1212; the month is an ordering device. Coordinate corrected to the hermitage southeast of Assisi on the lower slope of Subasio, some 3.4 km from the figure in the research pool, which sat on the wrong flank of the mountain.
stops.campa: The Benedictine house is safe and it is not what she came out of Assisi for. Those nuns own land, take dowries, and seat the choir by birth, which is the arrangement she has just climbed out of a walled-up door to escape. So she goes further out. Sant'Angelo di Panzo sits on the lower slope southeast of the city, a smaller settlement of religious women with less institution about it and nothing much to keep her there. She is at Panzo a matter of weeks before she moves again.
sources: OpenStreetMap Nominatim, "Sant'Angelo di Panzo, San Vitale, Assisi"
suggested_refs: The site of Sant'Angelo di Panzo on the lower southeast slope of Monte Subasio

stops.name: Sant'Angelo di Panzo, Agnes taken by the hair
stops.date_confidence: attested that Clare's sister Caterina joined her sixteen days after the flight and was renamed Agnes; the date is that count applied to 18 March. The family's violent attempt to seize her is attested in the 1253 depositions. The dead weight of her body and the withering of Monaldo's arm are faith claims and are reconstruction.
stops.campa: Sixteen days after Clare's flight her younger sister Caterina walks out of the same house and follows her. The family comes again, a dozen of them, and this time they do not argue. They take the girl by the hair and drag her down the hillside. The sisters testify at the inquiry that her body grew too heavy to carry and that Monaldo's raised fist went dead in the air before it landed. What nobody disputes is the beating, or that she stayed. Francis cuts her hair as well and gives her the name Agnes.
suggested_refs: Acts of the Process of Canonisation of Saint Clare, 1253, depositions of the sisters of San Damiano

segments.name: The Poor Ladies of San Damiano

stops.name: San Damiano, the ruined church given to the women
stops.date_confidence: inferred. Sources give the settlement at San Damiano variously as c. 1212 (Wikipedia, 'San Damiano, Assisi') and 1216 (Wikipedia, 'Poor Clares'). Not resolved. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from saint_francis.journey.json rather than re-geocoded.
stops.campa: Francis gives them San Damiano, the small church below the walls whose stones he carried on his own back six years earlier, and where he says a painted Christ once spoke to him. There is a chapel, a dormitory over it, a strip of garden, and a wall. Clare will be inside that wall for forty-one years and will not, as far as any record shows, sleep a night anywhere else. The community takes the name Poor Ladies. It owns no property and takes no dowries. What the sisters eat is what the friars carry back from begging in Assisi that day.
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stops 'San Damiano, the crucifix speaks' and 'San Damiano, stones for a reward'
suggested_refs: The convent of San Damiano below Assisi, preserved with the sisters' refectory and dormitory

stops.name: San Damiano, the office she does not want
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, flagged not resolved. The Catholic Encyclopedia dates her appointment as superior to 1215, Wikipedia to 1216, Franciscan Media only to 'age 21'. 1215 chosen for ordering. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Francis makes her superior of the house over her objection. She takes the title abbess because canon law offers her no other, and uses it as little as she can get away with. Witnesses at the inquiry describe her washing the feet of the sisters who come in from the roads and drying them with her own veil, emptying the pallets of the sick, keeping the worst bed in the dormitory for herself. She will govern for nearly forty years. The year she starts is not agreed on by the three sources that give one.
suggested_refs: Catherine M. Mooney, Clare of Assisi and the Thirteenth-Century Church (2016), on Clare's exercise of the abbatial office

stops.name: San Damiano, word of the Lateran clause
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Fourth Lateran decree of 1215. Clare was not at Rome and the stop stands at her own pin: what is dated here is the constraint arriving at San Damiano, not a journey. Day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Word comes up from Rome that the Fourth Lateran Council has forbidden the founding of religious orders under new rules. Anything new must be fitted inside a rule already approved. For a house whose entire content is a way of living that has never been written down, this is not an administrative detail. The clause is enacted this autumn by men in Rome who have never heard her name. She will work against it for the next thirty-eight years: letters to four popes, endowments turned away at the gate of a house with no income.
suggested_refs: Canon 13 of the Fourth Lateran Council, 1215, forbidding new religious rules

stops.name: San Damiano, the daughter houses go out
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Perugia foundation and the rapid spread to Florence, Venice, Mantua and Padua (Wikipedia, 'Poor Clares'). Month and day defaulted. The stop is at San Damiano because Clare never went to any of them.
stops.campa: A house of Poor Ladies opens at Perugia, and then quickly at Florence, Venice, Mantua, Padua. Clare travels to none of them and never sets eyes on any of them. Women who have never laid eyes on her take up a way of life she is still improvising inside one walled garden below Assisi. In Rome the cardinals begin handling the thing as an order, something that will need administering, visitors, a uniform text written for houses none of them has seen. Clare is twenty-four years old.
suggested_refs: The early Damianite foundations at Perugia, Florence, Venice, Mantua and Padua

stops.name: San Damiano, Ugolino writes them a rule
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Catholic Encyclopedia for a forma vitae drafted by Cardinal Ugolino during Francis's absence in the East; month and day defaulted. The characterisation of its Benedictine substance is standard in the literature and was not checked against the Latin text, which was not reachable.
stops.campa: Cardinal Ugolino of Ostia, protector of the Franciscans, writes a rule for the women while Francis is away in Egypt. It is a Benedictine rule with Franciscan trimming: strict enclosure, obedience, silence, and the settled assumption that a house of nuns must have an income to live on. Clare accepts the enclosure and the silence and the obedience. On the income she does not move, and she will not move on it for the rest of her life. In 1227 Ugolino is elected pope and takes the name Gregory IX.
suggested_refs: Ugolino's forma vitae for the Damianite houses, c. 1219

stops.name: San Damiano, the cell of reeds and the Canticle
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Francis's stay in a cell by San Damiano and the composition of the Canticle there are carried by the Franciscan tradition; Clare's proximity is secure, the specific nursing attributed to her is not. Date inherited from saint_francis.journey.json to keep the two files aligned.
stops.campa: Francis comes down from the mountain half blind, unable to bear daylight, and is put in a cell of reeds beside San Damiano because there is nowhere better and because Clare is there. He lies fifty days in the dark with mice running over him. Out of that spring comes the Canticle of the Creatures, the first great poem written in Italian, made a few yards from the wall of her house while her sisters keep him fed. He writes verses for them too, telling them to live in truth and to want nothing besides.
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'San Damiano, the Canticle of the Creatures'
suggested_refs: The Canticum Creaturarum and Francis's Audite Poverelle, both composed at San Damiano in 1225

stops.name: San Damiano, the coffin at the grille
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The diversion of Francis's funeral procession to the window of San Damiano is recorded in the official Legend, composed decades after the event, not in any contemporaneous account. Date inherited from saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: He dies at the Porziuncola on the third of October. The next morning the procession carrying his body up to Assisi turns aside at San Damiano, and the coffin is brought to the window through which the sisters take communion. The grille is opened. Clare and her women look at him and kiss the pierced hands. She is thirty-two years old and has twenty-seven years still to live, none of which she will spend outside this wall. Then the procession re-forms and goes on up the hill to San Giorgio.
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'Assisi, San Giorgio, the burial, and the window of San Damiano'
suggested_refs: The communion window of San Damiano, shown to pilgrims as the site of the 1226 farewell

stops.name: San Damiano, the illness that does not lift
stops.date_confidence: inferred. Franciscan Media gives twenty-seven years of serious illness before her death, which counts back to 1226; the research pool elsewhere inflated this to 'roughly three decades' from 'c. 1224/25' and that reading is rejected here. Month and day are an ordering device.
stops.campa: From about this year she is ill and does not recover. The record gives twenty-seven years, counted backward from her death, of a sickness never named in any source beyond its effects: she cannot stand, cannot walk the cloister, cannot get to the church for the office. She governs the house from the bed for more than half her time in office. Propped up on it, she spins linen, and turns out more than fifty corporals for the poor churches of the valley, the linen cloth that goes under the bread at Mass.
suggested_refs: The corporals attributed to Clare's own spinning, preserved at the Protomonastero di Santa Chiara, Assisi

stops.name: San Damiano, the pope offers to release her
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The exchange is reported by the Catholic Encyclopedia and repeated on Wikipedia in a different English wording that does not agree with it; neither was traced to a primary edition. The date places it in the visit that produced the bull of 17 September 1228.
stops.campa: Gregory IX comes to Assisi to canonise Francis and comes down the hill to San Damiano to see the woman he has been arguing with by letter for a decade. He puts it to her kindly. The house is destitute, the times are dangerous, and a pope can loose a nun from a vow she made when she was very young. She answers that she wants absolution from her sins and no absolution whatever from following Christ. He drops it. Two English versions of that sentence survive and they do not match.
stops.quote: Holy Father, I crave for absolution from my sins, but I desire not to be absolved from the obligation of following Jesus Christ
stops.quote_source: Attributed reply of Clare to Pope Gregory IX, Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Saint Clare of Assisi' (newadvent.org); Wikipedia renders the same episode as 'never and in no way do I wish to be dispensed from following Christ'
suggested_refs: The two divergent English translations of Clare's reply to Gregory IX, unreconciled

stops.name: San Damiano, Sicut manifestum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Catholic Encyclopedia. A broader framing on Wikipedia spreads the securing of the poverty privileges across roughly 1228 to 1240 through successive popes; the two accounts are not reconciled and the single dated bull is used here.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of September the bull is issued. It addresses her as the daughter of Favarone and states that no one may compel her or her sisters to receive possessions. She has extracted from the papacy a written guarantee of the right to own nothing, which is the exact reverse of what every religious house in Christendom asks Rome for. An earlier privilege of the same kind is traditionally credited to Innocent III in 1216, but no original survives and the historians argue about whether it existed.
stops.quote: It is evident that the desire of consecrating yourselves to God alone has led you to abandon every wish for temporal things.
stops.quote_source: Pope Gregory IX, Privilegium Paupertatis, 1228, English translation via newadvent.org
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Saint Clare of Assisi': '1228 - September 17: Received the Privilegium Paupertatis'
suggested_refs: The bull Sicut manifestum, 17 September 1228, and the disputed Innocentian privilege of 1216

stops.name: San Damiano, the first letter to Prague
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1234 as the date of the first surviving letter to Agnes of Prague; month and day defaulted. Wikipedia's article on Agnes confirms a correspondence running over two decades and that the two women never met.
stops.campa: A king's daughter in Bohemia has refused an emperor and a king and shut herself into a monastery she built next to the hospital she founded. Agnes of Prague writes to Assisi, and Clare answers. Clare writes to her about a mirror. Look into it every day, she says, and study your own face in it; the mirror is Christ on the wood. The exchange will run twenty years and four surviving letters, and the two of them never meet and never stand in the same country.
stops.quote: He, Christ, is the splendor of eternal glory, the brightness of eternal light, and the mirror without cloud.
stops.quote_source: Clare of Assisi, letter to Agnes of Prague, English translation quoted at catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The four letters of Clare to Agnes of Prague, in Armstrong, ed., Clare of Assisi: Early Documents. The Lady (2006)

stops.name: San Damiano, telling a princess to refuse the money
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The second and third letters are conventionally dated c. 1235-36 and 1238; the reading of them as a response to curial pressure on Agnes to accept endowment is the standard interpretation and was not checked against the Latin. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The curia leans on Prague to take an endowment. A royal foundation, the argument runs, cannot live on daily alms through a northern winter. Clare writes twice more and tells Agnes to hold. She is instructing a princess of Bohemia to refuse her own family's money on the strength of an arrangement that works in Umbria, where the friars beg every morning and the valley is full of bread. Whether it can work north of the Alps is a genuine question. Clare does not concede it in any of the four letters.
suggested_refs: The Convent of Saint Agnes, Prague, founded 1231, the first Poor Clare house north of the Alps

segments.name: The Wall and the Silver Box

stops.name: San Damiano, the ladders on the garden wall
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1240 by en.wikipedia and independently by it.wikipedia. The Catholic Encyclopedia's 1234 is an error and is dropped, not carried as an open alternative: Frederick II was reconciled with Gregory IX in 1234 and was not campaigning in Umbria; imperial war in the Papal States follows his excommunication of March 1239.
stops.campa: Frederick's mercenaries, whom the Latin sources call Saracens, come over the garden wall in September. The sisters wake to soldiers in the cloister, some of them young, some of them the daughters of the men who once came up the hill to drag Clare home. She has herself carried to the doorway holding a small box, ivory or silver, with the reserved bread inside it, and she prays out loud. The soldiers go back over the wall. Three centuries of painters will swap the box for a gold sunburst the size of a shield.
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Saint Clare of Assisi' (1234, rejected here)
suggested_refs: The pyx of San Damiano, and the later monstrance iconography that replaced it in Renaissance and Baroque painting

stops.name: Assisi, the army below the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested for the June 1241 threat to Assisi (en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia); the day 22 June is carried from the standard chronology. Clare's prayer as the cause of the withdrawal is the community's own account, given in the 1253 depositions, and is reconstruction.
stops.campa: In June of the following year an imperial force comes against Assisi itself and camps below the walls. Clare, who has not walked in fifteen years, sends ashes out to the sisters and has them put ashes on their own heads, and they pray through the night. The army goes away. The city that pulled down its imperial fortress in 1198 and swore it needed no lord above it credits the deliverance to an invalid in a convent outside its gate. Assisi keeps the twenty-second of June as a feast for it.
suggested_refs: The medieval circuit of the Assisi walls, and the 22 June feast kept in the city for the deliverance

stops.name: San Damiano, the rule she will not take
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1247 rule of Innocent IV from the general historical record; the primary text was not fetched for this file. The exact day is carried from the standard chronology and is the weakest element of the entry.
stops.campa: Innocent IV issues a new rule for the women's houses. It attaches them to the Friars Minor, which Clare has wanted for thirty years, and it permits them to hold property in common, which is the one thing she will not have. The two concessions come bound into a single text and cannot be prised apart. Across Italy other abbesses take it up gladly, and their reason is not obscure: the alternative is a house full of women living on whatever a town chooses to give them that morning. Clare does not obey it.
sources: General historical record of the 1247 curial act (primary text not fetched)
suggested_refs: The 1247 rule of Innocent IV for the Order of San Damiano

stops.name: San Damiano, writing her own text
stops.date_confidence: attested that a 1250 instruction allowed houses to keep their earlier observance; primary texts not fetched. That she began drafting her own Form of Life in consequence is inference from the 1252 approval, and month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: Three years on, facing houses that will not take the new rule and houses that will not give it up, the curia rules that a community may keep whatever observance it had before. It is a retreat, and it is the opening she has been waiting for. She stops petitioning against other people's texts and begins writing her own, taking the Franciscan rule of 1223 for its frame and setting into chapter six the clause about ownership she has been defending in correspondence for twenty-two years.
stops.quote: by not receiving or having possession or ownership either themselves or through an intermediary, or even anything that might reasonably be called ownership, except as much land as necessity requires for the integrity and proper seclusion of the monastery
stops.quote_source: Rule of Saint Clare, ch. 6, English translation, porziuncolaproject.com
sources: General historical record of the 1250 curial instruction (primary text not fetched)
Rule of Saint Clare, ch. 6, via porziuncolaproject.com
suggested_refs: Clare's Forma vitae, chapters 6 and 8, on holding nothing

stops.name: San Damiano, a cardinal's signature
stops.date_confidence: attested for 16 September 1252 as the date of Cardinal Rainaldo of Ostia's approval of the Form of Life, from the general historical record; the primary act was not fetched for this file.
stops.campa: Cardinal Rainaldo of Ostia, protector of the order, approves the Form of Life on the sixteenth of September. A cardinal's approval binds one house and can be revoked by the next cardinal to hold the office; it is not what she wants and she takes it anyway. Clare is fifty-eight and has been in bed for a quarter of a century, and she now sets about getting the only signature in Christendom that cannot be undone. Rainaldo himself will be pope inside three years. She has eleven months.
sources: General historical record of Rainaldo's 1252 approval (primary act not fetched)
suggested_refs: Cardinal Rainaldo of Ostia, later Pope Alexander IV, protector of the Order of San Damiano

stops.name: San Damiano, the last letter to Prague
stops.date_confidence: attested for early 1253; month and day defaulted. The quoted line is from an Italian rendering of the fourth letter published by the Protomonastero di Santa Chiara; the Latin original was not fetched.
stops.campa: The last letter to Prague is written by a dying woman to a woman she has never seen. It is not administrative and it settles nothing. It is about the crib and the cross, the King of the angels laid down in a feeding trough, and it asks Agnes to put herself into the mirror and stay there. Twenty years of correspondence end with neither of them ever crossing the Alps, and the four letters are all that is left of the friendship. Nothing Agnes wrote back survives.
stops.quote: Il Re degli angeli, il Signore del cielo e della terra e reclinato in una mangiatoia
stops.quote_source: Clare of Assisi, Fourth Letter to Agnes of Prague, Italian text published at assisisantachiara.it
suggested_refs: The fourth letter to Agnes of Prague, early 1253

stops.name: San Damiano, the Testament and the Blessing
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Testament and Blessing belong to this period; month and day are an ordering device. The authenticity of both texts has been challenged in twentieth-century scholarship and that debate is not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: In these same months she dictates, or has scribes finish, a Testament and a Blessing for the sisters who will come after her. The Testament goes back over how the thing began: Francis standing on the wall of this church years before there were any women in it, calling out in French that ladies would live here whose fame would glorify the whole Church. Whether either text is really hers has been fought over hard for a hundred years, and the argument has not been settled by anybody yet.
stops.quote: Lo stesso Signore, che ci ha donato un buon inizio, ci doni ancora di crescere nel bene e di perseverarvi fino alla fine. Amen.
stops.quote_source: Testament of Clare of Assisi, Italian text published at assisisantachiara.it
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'San Damiano, stones for a reward', sourced to the Testament of St. Clare
suggested_refs: The Testament and the Blessing of Clare, and the twentieth-century debate over their authenticity

stops.name: San Damiano, Solet annuere
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The claim in the research pool and on Wikipedia's 'Poor Clares' page that the bull came one day before her death is arithmetically wrong: the bull is dated 9 August, she died on 11 August. it.wikipedia has it right.
stops.campa: Innocent IV is in Assisi and she is dying. On the ninth of August he seals the bull Solet annuere, confirming her Form of Life for the Order of San Damiano. It is the first rule written by a woman for women that ever carried a papal seal, and it is granted to one house, hers, with the quarrel over the rest of the order left standing. Chapter one begins where she began, out on the plain in the dark with the friars and the shears: obedience, chastity, and nothing of one's own. The seal is lead on a silk cord.
stops.quote: The form of life of the Order of the Poor Sisters that Blessed Francis established is this: to observe the Holy Gospel of Our Lord Jesus Christ, by living in obedience, without anything of one's own, and in chastity.
stops.quote_source: Rule of Saint Clare, ch. 1, English translation, porziuncolaproject.com
sources: Rule of Saint Clare via porziuncolaproject.com
suggested_refs: The bull Solet annuere, 9 August 1253, preserved at the Protomonastero di Santa Chiara

stops.name: San Damiano, the seal brought to the bed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The tradition that the sealed bull was placed in her hands on 10 August is a separate later claim and must not be conflated with the bull's own date of 9 August. The quoted Umbrian line is given secondhand on a devotional site; the primary edition was not fetched.
stops.campa: The sealed parchment is carried out to San Damiano and put into her hands. A witness at the inquiry remembers that she lifted it to her mouth and kissed it. She has been arguing with the Roman curia for forty-one years, through four popes, and this is the object at the end of the argument: wax, cord, and a page confirming that she may keep nothing. She is too weak to sit up in the bed. The sisters hold the parchment steady for her while she does it, and then it is carried off and put away with the papers of the house.
stops.quote: medesima se puse quella bolla alla bocca sua per basciarla
stops.quote_source: Older Italian, quoted at ora-et-labora.net from the Process and Legend tradition, describing Clare kissing the sealed bull of her Rule
sources: ora-et-labora.net, 'Regola di Santa Chiara e biografia'
suggested_refs: Acts of the Process of Canonisation of Saint Clare, 1253, on the reception of the bull

stops.name: San Damiano, the eleventh of August
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the death; age given as fifty-nine. The last words and the exchange about speaking to her soul are traditional, traced only to secondary retellings and to a summary of the depositions of Sister Benvenuta and Sister Anastasia, not to a primary edition.
stops.campa: She is fifty-nine years old and has been inside the wall of San Damiano for forty-one of them, in the room Francis put her in at eighteen. The sisters, watching her lips move, ask whom she is talking to, and she tells them she is talking to her soul. Then she tells the soul to go: go safely, you have a good escort, He who made you has made you holy and has always guarded you and loves you as a mother loves her child. Blessed be You, O God, for having created me.
stops.quote: Go forth in peace, for you have followed the good road. Go forth without fear, for he who created you has made you holy, has always protected you, and loves you as a mother. Blessed be you, my God, for having created me.
stops.quote_source: Attributed last words of Clare, quoted at catholicsaints.info and repeated on Wikipedia, 'Clare of Assisi'
sources: franciscanmedia.org, 'St. Clare, Light of Assisi' (for 'I am speaking to my soul', itself secondhand)
suggested_refs: The depositions of Sister Benvenuta and Sister Anastasia in the 1253 process

stops.name: Assisi, San Giorgio: carried up the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was buried at San Giorgio, inside the walls, out of fear that the body would be stolen; the day after death is inference. Coordinate inherited from saint_francis.journey.json, which uses this pin for San Giorgio; the research pool's 43.0713/12.6133 lands near the Piazza del Comune and is wrong.
stops.campa: A holy body is worth money and can be carried off, and Assisi has already had to build a fortress of a basilica to keep Francis's bones from being stolen. The commune does not leave Clare outside the wall. Under guard, with the pope in the procession, she is carried up the hill and into the city she left one night in March forty-one years earlier, and laid in San Giorgio, where Francis had lain before her and where he had gone to school as a boy.
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'Assisi, San Giorgio, the burial, and the window of San Damiano'
pica_bourlemont.journey.json, on the school of the canons of San Giorgio
suggested_refs: The church of San Giorgio, Assisi, absorbed into the Basilica di Santa Chiara after 1257

stops.name: San Damiano, the sisters are put on oath
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to detail. The inquiry of 28-29 November 1253 under Bishop Bartolomeo of Spoleto is standard in the literature; the original transcript was not fetched for this file, and the surviving Latin is itself a later translation of a lost vernacular original.
stops.campa: In late November the bishop of Spoleto sits at San Damiano and takes sworn evidence, first from the sisters and then from relatives and townspeople out of Assisi. They speak in Umbrian and are recorded in Umbrian, and the Latin that survives is a translation made afterward from a vernacular original now lost. Nearly everything anyone knows about her hands, her bed, her temper and the night at Bastia comes out of these two days, from women who had shared one roof with her for four decades.
sources: General historical record of the 1253 canonisation process (transcript not fetched)
suggested_refs: Acts of the Process of Canonisation of Saint Clare, 28-29 November 1253, in Armstrong, ed., The Lady (2006)

stops.name: Assisi, the cross carried up from San Damiano
stops.date_confidence: traditional for the 1257 date of the community's move into the city; month and day defaulted. That the original San Damiano cross now hangs in the Basilica di Santa Chiara and a replica hangs at San Damiano is attested.
stops.campa: The sisters leave San Damiano and move up into the city beside the rising basilica, and they take the painted cross with them, the Romanesque panel from which Francis said he heard a voice in 1205. It hangs now in a chapel of Santa Chiara. Down at San Damiano, in the empty church, hangs a copy. In 1263 Urban IV will give the whole order her name and permit its houses to own land, which is the one provision she spent her life keeping out of the text.
suggested_refs: The San Damiano crucifix, Cappella del Crocifisso, Basilica di Santa Chiara, Assisi

stops.name: Assisi, buried under the high altar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the translation of 3 October 1260. The canonisation is attested for 26 September 1255 at Anagni; en.wikipedia's 'Clare of Assisi' article wrongly places it at Rome, while its 'Anagni Cathedral' article and it.wikipedia give Anagni, which is followed here. No stop is staged at Anagni: Clare was two years dead and never went there.
stops.campa: Alexander IV had canonised her at Anagni on the twenty-sixth of September 1255, by the bull Clara claris praeclara, and a basilica has been going up over San Giorgio ever since, banded in the white and pink stone of Subasio. On the third of October 1260, seven years after she was carried up the hill, the body is brought out of the old church and buried under the high altar of the new one. Then the grave is closed, and where exactly it lies is not written down. That part is deliberate.
suggested_refs: The bull Clara claris praeclara, Anagni, 26 September 1255

stops.name: Assisi, the coffin opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Wikipedia's article on the Basilica of Saint Clare. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives only 1850. The finding of an intact skeleton with flesh and clothing decayed to dust is what the excavation reports, against the popular claim of an incorrupt visible body.
stops.campa: Six centuries later they dig for her. On the twenty-third of September 1850 the searchers reach the coffin and open it. The burial cloth and the flesh have gone to dust and the skeleton is entire. The popular account, that she lies uncorrupted and visible just as she was on the day she died, does not survive contact with the excavation. What pilgrims are shown today is a made figure, wax laid over the bones, and the bones themselves are behind a grate.
suggested_refs: The 1850 exhumation report and the wax effigy displayed in the crypt of Santa Chiara

stops.name: Assisi, the crypt of Santa Chiara
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Wikipedia's article on the Basilica of Saint Clare for the 1872 translation by Gioacchino Pecci. it.wikipedia instead dates the crypt's neo-Gothic restyling to 1935 and does not mention 1872; the discrepancy is flagged, not resolved.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of September 1872 the archbishop of Perugia, Gioacchino Pecci, six years short of the papacy he will hold as Leo XIII, lays the bones in a shrine cut under the basilica. The crypt is neo-Gothic, lit and railed for visitors who come down the stairs in a queue, and it is restyled again in the following century. The Italian and the English accounts of that work do not give the same date for it and have never been reconciled. She is on view.
stops.quote: Let the sisters not appropriate anything to themselves, neither a house nor a place nor anything at all; instead, as pilgrims and strangers in this world who serve the Lord in poverty and humility, let them confidently send for alms.
stops.quote_source: Rule of Saint Clare, ch. 8, English translation, porziuncolaproject.com
sources: Rule of Saint Clare via porziuncolaproject.com
suggested_refs: The neo-Gothic crypt of the Basilica di Santa Chiara, built 1850, restyled 1935

stops.name: San Damiano, patroness of television
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1958 for the declaration by Pius XII; the exact date of the act was not in the material reachable for this file, and month and day are defaulted. The Christmas vision on which it rests is Legend material and is not independently attested.
stops.campa: Pius XII names her the heavenly patroness of television. The reason given is an episode out of the Legend: on a Christmas night, too ill to be carried to the friars' church for the office, she saw and heard the whole of it from her bed at San Damiano, the singing, the altar, the crib. Seven hundred years on, the Vatican reads that as a description of remote vision and hands her the medium. The bed is a few yards from the window where they brought Francis in his coffin.
sources: Legend of Saint Clare, via secondary summary
suggested_refs: Pius XII's 1958 declaration of Clare as patroness of television
